Qing dynasty military commander Nian Gengyao's history

Nian Gengrao based on Nian Gengyao whose courtesy name was Lianggoing was a Chinese military commander of the Qing armies in the northwest.
He was born a member of the Han Chinese Bordered Yellow Banner and had a lot of military experience on the western frontier of the Qing Empire.
He helped to incorporate the region that is now know as Qinghai into the Qing Empire.
His father, Nian Xialing served as Viceroy of Huguang.
In March 1709, the Nian family was assigned to serve Prince Yinzhen who later became the Yongzhen Emperor.
Around the same time, his sister, Imperial noble Consort Dunsu, (who was the inspiration for Nian Shuyan) became Yinzhen’s concubine.
In October 1709, he was appointed as Governor of Sichuan and was gradually noticed by the Kangxi Emperor.
In the 16 years of his administration, he suppressed several uprisings of the natives west of Sichuan.
In 1718, he was made Governor-General of Sichuan and was given the power to direct military affairs.
As General Who Secures the Westm Nian Gengyao was active in supplying Yinti’s campaign in Tibet against Tsewang Rabtan.
In June 1721, he was granted an audience with the old Kangxi Emperor at Rehe and was promoted.
In December 1722, the Kangxi Emperor passed away and Yinzhen ascended as the Youngzheng Emperor.
He granted an audience to Nian Gengyao early in 1723 and gave him a minor hereditary rank and the title of Grand Guardian and made Gengyao’s older brother, Nian Xiyao, Governor of Guangdong.
A few months later, as a reward for aiding the Yongzheng Emperor in getting rid of the Dzungars from Tibet, Nian was elevated to a third-class duke.
The emperor was informal with him and promoted friendship between Longkodo and Nian.
In 1723, Nian became commander-in-chief of the forces suppressing the Khoshotes of Qinghai.
With the help of general Yue Zhongqi, Nian won several victorals over the rebels and suppressed the revolt in a few months, adding Qinghai to the Qing Emperor.
He was promoted to a first-class Duke.
When he made a visit to Beijin in late 1724 and paid his respects to the Yongzheng Emperor, he was given additional privileges normally given to a Prince of the First Rank.
His attitude created jealousy and hatred and many officials submitted memorials against him.
He was not slow to find that he lost imperial favor because on his return to Xi’an in January 1725, he submitted a memorial imploring the Yongzheng Emperor’s mercy.
Meanwhile, it was discovered that he had been exchanging secret correspondence with Yintang, the emperor’s brother and political rival.
His plea for leave was denied and at the end of May, he was transferred to the post of Tartar General at Hangzhou.
The armies he once commanded was now controlled by Yue Zhongqi.
Accusations against him accumulated from his former friends and officials and in a few months, he continued to be demoted until he was a bannerman-at-large.
In November, he was arrested and taken under escort to Beijing.
Early in 1725, his crimes were counted under 92 heads and he was sentenced to execution.
The Yongzheng Emperor gave him the privilege of committing suicide but his eldest son, Nian Fu, was beheaded and his sons were banished.
He was married to Aisin GIoro’s daughter and to the Manchu Plain Yellow Bannerman Nalan Xingde’s daughter.
Tuhai was a Manchu Bannerman and general of the Green Standard Army and a great minister who existed during the Qing Dynasty.
In the 8th year (1651), he worked as a scholar of the Nei secretariat of the library then he became a minister of the government.
After Emperor Kangxi succeeded to the throne, he received the Manchu doctorate of Zheng Huang.
In the 2nd year of Kangxi (1663), he had the merit of suppressing the forces of "reversing Qing and subduing the Ming." He was promoted to the First rank of Qing cha Du lieutenant.
In the 14th year (1675), he was made Vice General, under the Prince of Xin, Fu Yuan.
In the 15th year (1676), he was promoted to general.
In the early years of Yongzheng, he was awarded the title of Duke of Zhongda.
In the 20th year (1681), he passed away at an unknown age.
